decks.title: Rights in the Indian Constitution, Part 1: Fundamental Rights
goals: Define a right, a bill of rights and justiciable
Explain the six categories of Fundamental Rights and their Articles
Explain Article 32 and the five writs
State the position of the right to property and the role of the National Human Rights Commission

slides.heading: Fundamental Rights
slides.body_md: Part 1: what **rights** are, the **six categories** of Fundamental Rights, and the **writs** that protect them.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what is a right, six categories, constitutional remedies, writs, and property and the Commission
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: A right is only worth something if it can be claimed. In this part we meet the Fundamental Rights of the Indian Constitution, look at the six categories one by one, and see how a citizen can go to court when a right is violated. We also look at the right to property and at the National Human Rights Commission.

slides.heading: What is a right?

rows: Right
A claim recognised by society and by law
Bill of rights
A list of rights in a constitution that the government cannot violate
Fundamental Rights
The rights in Part III of the Constitution
Justiciable
Enforceable by a court of law

visual.alt: Table of terms: a right is a claim recognised by society and law; a bill of rights is a list of rights in a constitution the government cannot violate; Fundamental Rights are in Part III; justiciable means enforceable by a court

slides.narration: A right is a claim that society and the law recognise. A bill of rights is a list of such rights in a constitution which the government is not allowed to violate. In India, this list is called the Fundamental Rights and is found in Part three of the Constitution. These rights are justiciable, which means that a court can enforce them.

visual.alt: Chart of the six categories of Fundamental Rights with their Articles: Right to Equality, Articles 14 to 18; Right to Freedom, 19 to 22; Right against Exploitation, 23 and 24; Right to Freedom of Religion, 25 to 28; Cultural and Educational Rights, 29 and 30; Right to Constitutional Remedies, Article 32
visual.caption: The six categories of Fundamental Rights in Part III.

slides.narration: The Fundamental Rights fall into six groups. Equality covers Articles fourteen to eighteen. Freedom covers nineteen to twenty two. Exploitation is twenty three and twenty four. Religion is twenty five to twenty eight. Cultural and educational rights are twenty nine and thirty. The last group, constitutional remedies, is Article thirty two, which lets people go to court.

slides.heading: Right to Equality

rows: Equality before law and equal protection of the laws
No discrimination by religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
Equality of opportunity in public employment
Abolition of untouchability
Abolition of titles

visual.alt: Table of the Right to Equality: Article 14 equality before law; 15 no discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth; 16 equal opportunity in public employment; 17 abolition of untouchability; 18 abolition of titles

slides.narration: Article fourteen says everyone is equal before the law and has equal protection of the laws. Article fifteen bars discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. Article sixteen gives equal opportunity in public employment. Article seventeen abolishes untouchability, and Article eighteen abolishes titles. Special provisions for women, children and backward groups are allowed.

slides.heading: Quick check: which right?
slides.body_md: A restaurant owner refuses to serve a customer because of caste. Which right is violated?
slides.narration: Think about which category deals with discrimination on grounds such as caste.

slides.heading: Right to Freedom: Article 19

rows: Speech and expression
A student writes a letter to a newspaper
Assembly (peaceful, unarmed)
Residents meet in a hall to discuss a road
Association
Workers form a union or a club
Movement and residence
A family moves to another state
Profession
A woman opens her own bakery

visual.alt: Table of Article 19 freedoms with daily-life examples: speech and expression, peaceful assembly, association, movement and residence, and profession; all subject to reasonable restrictions
visual.caption: All subject to reasonable restrictions such as public order.

slides.narration: Article nineteen gives citizens six freedoms: speech and expression, peaceful assembly without arms, forming associations, moving freely and living in any part of the country, and following a profession. They are not absolute. The State may place reasonable restrictions, for example for public order or the security of the State, so that one person's freedom does not harm others.

slides.heading: Articles 20, 21, 21A and 22

rows: Protection in respect of conviction for offences
Protection of life and personal liberty
Free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 (86th Amendment, 2002)
Protection against arbitrary arrest and detention, including rules on preventive detention

visual.alt: Table of Articles 20 to 22: protection in respect of conviction, protection of life and personal liberty, education for children aged 6 to 14 added in 2002, and protection against arbitrary arrest and detention

slides.narration: Article twenty protects a person from unfair punishment for an offence. Article twenty one protects life and personal liberty. Article twenty one A, added by the eighty sixth Amendment in two thousand two, gives children aged six to fourteen free and compulsory education. Article twenty two protects against arbitrary arrest and detention, with special rules for preventive detention.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: applying Article 22
slides.body_md: Kavita's brother is arrested in the imagined town of Nandanpur. List the safeguards that must be followed.
bullets: He may **consult a lawyer** of choice
He must be **produced before a magistrate within 24 hours**

rows: Tell the person the grounds of the arrest
Allow the person to consult a lawyer of choice
Produce the person before a magistrate within 24 hours, excluding travel time
No longer detention without the magistrate's order

visual.alt: Worked example table of safeguards on arrest: grounds told, a lawyer of choice, production before a magistrate within twenty-four hours excluding travel time, and no longer detention without the magistrate's order
visual.caption: Applied to an imagined arrest in the town of Nandanpur.

slides.narration: Let us apply Article twenty two to an imagined arrest. First, the police must tell the person why he is arrested. Second, he may consult a lawyer of his choice. Third, he must be produced before a magistrate within twenty four hours, not counting travel time. Without the magistrate's order he cannot be held longer. Preventive detention follows special rules.

slides.heading: Right against Exploitation

rows: Traffic in human beings and forced labour (begar)
Employing children below 14 in factories, mines and hazardous work

visual.alt: Table of the Right against Exploitation: Article 23 prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour; Article 24 prohibits employing children below fourteen in factories, mines and hazardous work

slides.narration: Article twenty three prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour, called begar. Someone made to work without pay because of a debt is a victim of this wrong. Article twenty four prohibits employing children below fourteen years in factories, mines and other hazardous work. Together the two Articles protect the weakest from being treated as goods.

slides.heading: Religion, culture and education

rows: Freedom of Religion (25 to 28)
Profess, practise, propagate; manage religious affairs; no tax for a religion; no compulsory religious instruction in a fully State-funded institution
Cultural and Educational (29 and 30)
Any section may protect its language, script and culture; minorities may set up and run educational institutions

visual.alt: Table of two rights: Freedom of Religion, Articles 25 to 28, with practice, management of affairs and no compulsion; Cultural and Educational Rights, Articles 29 and 30, with protection of language and culture and the minorities' right to run institutions

slides.narration: Articles twenty five to twenty eight protect freedom of religion. A person may profess, practise and propagate a religion, subject to public order, morality and health. No one can be forced to pay tax for a religion, or to join religious worship in an institution funded wholly by the State. Articles twenty nine and thirty protect language and culture, and let minorities run their own educational institutions.

slides.heading: Right to Constitutional Remedies

nodes.label: Person moves the Supreme Court (Article 32) or a High Court (Article 226)

visual.alt: Flow: a Fundamental Right is violated, the person moves the Supreme Court under Article 32 or a High Court under Article 226, the court issues a writ, and the authority must obey
visual.caption: How the remedy works

slides.narration: A right without a remedy is only words. Article thirty two lets a person go straight to the Supreme Court when a Fundamental Right is violated, and Article two twenty six gives the High Courts a similar power. Dr Ambedkar regarded Article thirty two as the most important Article, because it makes the other rights real. The court issues writs to enforce rights.

visual.alt: Chart of the five writs: habeas corpus, to have the body, produce a detained person in court; mandamus, we command, an official must do a legal duty; prohibition, stop a lower court going beyond its power; quo warranto, by what authority, tests a claim to a public office; certiorari, quash an order a lower body made without authority
visual.caption: The five writs at a glance.

slides.narration: A writ is a written order of a court. Habeas corpus orders that a detained person be produced before the court. Mandamus orders an official to do a legal duty. Prohibition stops a lower court from going beyond its power. Quo warranto asks by what authority someone holds a public office. Certiorari quashes an order that a lower body passed without authority.

slides.heading: Quick check: which writ?
slides.body_md: A mother says her son is held in an unknown place with no charge. Which writ should she seek?
slides.narration: Think about the writ that asks the court to see the person held.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: matching writs
slides.body_md: Match each imagined situation to the writ the court would use.

rows: A man is held at a police post for two days with no charge
Habeas corpus
A clerk refuses to issue a ration card the law requires him to give
Mandamus
A tribunal starts hearing a case outside its powers
Prohibition
A person holds a post without the required qualification
Quo warranto
A lower body has passed an order without authority
Certiorari

visual.alt: Worked example table matching situations to writs: detention without charge to habeas corpus; a clerk refusing his duty to mandamus; a tribunal beyond its powers to prohibition; a post held without qualification to quo warranto; an order passed without authority to certiorari
visual.caption: Match the situation to the writ.

slides.narration: Read each situation and ask what the court needs to do. If a person is held without charge, the court asks for the person: habeas corpus. If an official ignores a duty, it commands him: mandamus. If a tribunal goes beyond its powers, the court stops it: prohibition. If a post is held without qualification, the court questions the holder: quo warranto. If an order is bad, it quashes it: certiorari.

slides.heading: The right to property

nodes.label: The 44th Amendment, 1978, removes it from Part III
Now a legal right under Article 300A

visual.alt: Flow: property was a Fundamental Right, land reform laws were challenged, the 44th Amendment of 1978 removed it from Part III, and it is now a legal right under Article 300A
visual.caption: The right to property

slides.narration: The Constitution first listed the right to property among the Fundamental Rights. Land reform laws, which aimed at fairer distribution of land, were challenged as violating this right. The forty fourth Amendment of nineteen seventy eight removed it from Part three. Today it is a legal, or constitutional, right under Article three hundred A: property can be taken only by authority of law.

slides.heading: The National Human Rights Commission

rows: Set up
Does
Inquires into violations of human rights, recommends action, spreads awareness
Cannot do
Punish; punishment is for the courts

visual.alt: Table about the National Human Rights Commission: set up in 1993; it inquires into violations, recommends action and spreads awareness; it cannot punish

slides.narration: The National Human Rights Commission was set up in nineteen ninety three. It inquires into complaints of violation of human rights, recommends action to the authorities, and works to spread awareness. It cannot itself punish anyone; punishing is the work of the courts. It supports, but does not replace, the remedies in Articles thirty two and two twenty six.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Meaning
Rights are claims; Part III rights are justiciable
Six categories
Equality, Freedom, Exploitation, Religion, Cultural and Educational, Remedies
Remedy
Article 32 and Article 226; five writs
Other

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: meaning of rights, six categories, remedies through Articles 32 and 226 and five writs, property under Article 300A and the Commission of 1993

slides.narration: To sum up. Rights are claims recognised by society and law, and the Fundamental Rights of Part three are justiciable. There are six categories. Citizens can go to the Supreme Court under Article thirty two and to the High Courts under Article two twenty six, and the courts issue five writs. Property is now a legal right, and the Commission of nineteen ninety three recommends action on violations.

Define each writ in **one line**, then give a situation
Support each point with an example

Property is a legal right under Article 300A since 1978

visual.alt: Table of common mistakes in Part 1 and what to write instead

slides.narration: A few tips. Always give the Article number with each right. Define each writ in one line and then give a situation that shows it. For property, remember the forty fourth Amendment of nineteen seventy eight and Article three hundred A. And in longer answers, support each point with a short example.

decks.title: Rights in the Indian Constitution, Part 2: Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties
goals: Explain the Directive Principles and why they are non-justiciable
Describe the groups of Directive Principles with examples
Relate Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles
State the Fundamental Duties and how they were added

slides.heading: Directive Principles and Duties
slides.body_md: Part 2: the **Directive Principles** of Part IV, how they relate to **rights**, and the **Fundamental Duties**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: what the principles are, groups and examples, rights and principles, conflict and harmony, and Fundamental Duties
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Rights protect individuals. But a country also needs goals to work for. In this part we study the Directive Principles of State Policy, which guide the government. We compare them with Fundamental Rights, see how conflict and harmony between them developed, and finish with the Fundamental Duties of citizens.

slides.heading: What are the Directive Principles?

rows: Where
Part IV of the Constitution, Articles 36 to 51
What
Guidelines for the government in making laws and policies
Force
Non-justiciable: courts cannot enforce them
Importance
Fundamental in the governance of the country

visual.alt: Table of Directive Principles: in Part IV, Articles 36 to 51; guidelines for laws and policies; non-justiciable; fundamental in governance

slides.narration: The Directive Principles are in Part four of the Constitution, from Article thirty six to fifty one. They are guidelines that the government is expected to follow in making laws and policies. They are non justiciable: a court cannot enforce them. Even so, the Constitution calls them fundamental in the governance of the country.

slides.heading: Groups of Directive Principles

rows: Goals
Welfare of the people; justice; better living standards; fair distribution of resources; international peace
Policies
Uniform civil code; prohibition of intoxicants; cottage industries; care of useful cattle; village panchayats
Non-justiciable rights
Adequate livelihood; equal pay for equal work; right to work; early childhood care below six

visual.alt: Table of the commonly taught groups of Directive Principles: goals, policies and non-justiciable rights, with examples of each

slides.narration: Textbooks usually place the principles in three groups. Goals are broad aims, such as the welfare of the people, justice, a better standard of living, fair distribution of resources and international peace. Policies guide laws, for example a uniform civil code, village panchayats and cottage industries. The third group, non justiciable rights, includes an adequate livelihood, equal pay for equal work and the right to work.

slides.heading: Quick check: spot the principle
slides.body_md: A state passes a law to give village councils powers of self-government. What kind of provision is this?
slides.narration: Think about whether it is a right of individuals, a duty, or a guideline to the government.

slides.heading: Some principles by Article

rows: Adequate livelihood and equal pay for equal work, fair distribution of resources
Village panchayats as units of self-government
Work, education and public assistance
Cottage industries in rural areas
A uniform civil code (listed as one of the principles)
Early childhood care and education for children below six
Promotion of international peace

visual.alt: Table of Directive Principles by Article: 39 livelihood, equal pay and fair distribution; 40 village panchayats; 41 work, education and assistance; 43 cottage industries; 44 a uniform civil code; 45 early childhood care below six; 51 international peace

slides.narration: Here are some principles by Article. Article thirty nine covers an adequate livelihood, equal pay for equal work for men and women, and fair distribution of resources. Article forty is about village panchayats, and Article forty three about cottage industries. Article forty four lists a uniform civil code as one principle. Article forty five covers care and education for children below six, and Article fifty one covers international peace.

slides.body_md: Decide whether each imagined item is a **right**, a **principle**, a **duty** or a **writ**.
bullets: Who is addressed: the State or the citizen?
Can a court enforce it directly?

rows: The state of Marenpur frees a student detained without being told why
Fundamental Right (Article 22)

visual.alt: Worked example table classifying imagined items: freeing a person detained without grounds is a Fundamental Right; training centres for cottage industries is a Directive Principle; cleaning a riverbank is a Fundamental Duty; a court ordering a clerk is a writ
visual.caption: Ask: who is addressed, and can a court enforce it?

slides.narration: To classify, ask two questions. Who is addressed, the State or the citizen? And can a court enforce it directly? Freeing a person held without being told why is the Fundamental Right of Article twenty two. Training centres for cottage industries is a Directive Principle. A student cleaning a riverbank acts on a Fundamental Duty. A court ordering a clerk is a writ.

sections.heading: 1. Rights and the Fundamental Rights
sections.body_md:
A **right** is a claim that is recognised by society and by law. A **bill of rights** is a list of rights set out in a constitution, which the government cannot violate. In India, the **Fundamental Rights** are found in **Part III** of the Constitution (Articles 12 to 35).

They are **justiciable**: a person whose right is violated can go to a court, and the court can enforce the right. They restrain the government and protect individuals.

key_terms.definition_md: A claim recognised by society and protected by law.
A list of rights in a constitution which the government is not allowed to violate.
Capable of being enforced by a court of law.

sections.heading: 2. The six categories
sections.body_md:
- **Right to Equality (14 to 18):** equality before law and equal protection of the laws; no discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth; equality of opportunity in public employment; abolition of untouchability; abolition of titles.
- **Right to Freedom (19 to 22):** Article 19 freedoms of speech and expression, assembly, association, movement, residence and profession, subject to reasonable restrictions; protection in respect of conviction (20); protection of life and personal liberty (21); education for children aged 6 to 14 (21A, 86th Amendment, 2002); protection against arbitrary arrest and detention (22), including preventive detention.
- **Right against Exploitation (23 and 24):** prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour (begar); prohibition of employing children below 14 in factories, mines and hazardous work.
- **Right to Freedom of Religion (25 to 28):** freedom to profess, practise and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality and health; management of religious affairs; no tax for a religion; no compulsory religious instruction in a fully State-funded institution.
- **Cultural and Educational Rights (29 and 30):** protection of language, script and culture; the right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions.
- **Right to Constitutional Remedies (32):** the right to approach the Supreme Court for enforcement of the other rights.

key_terms.definition_md: Detention of a person on suspicion that he or she may act in a way harmful to security or public order, in order to prevent the act rather than to punish it.
Limits placed by law on a freedom, for example for public order, so that one person's freedom does not harm others.

sections.heading: 3. Constitutional remedies and writs
sections.body_md:
Under **Article 32** a person may go straight to the **Supreme Court**, and under **Article 226** to a **High Court**, when a Fundamental Right is violated. Dr Ambedkar regarded Article 32 as the most important Article, because without a remedy the other rights would have little meaning.

The courts issue **writs**, which are written orders. The five writs are shown below.

key_terms.definition_md: A written order of a court directing a person or authority to act or not to act.
A writ, meaning to have the body, ordering that a detained person be produced before the court so the legality of the detention can be examined.
A writ, meaning we command, ordering a public official or body to perform a legal duty.
A writ by which a higher court stops a lower court or tribunal from acting beyond its jurisdiction.
A writ, meaning by what authority, asking a person to show the legal authority to hold a public office.
A writ by which a higher court quashes an order that a lower court or tribunal passed without authority.

sections.heading: 4. Property and the Human Rights Commission
sections.body_md:
The right to property was at first a Fundamental Right. Land reform laws were challenged as violating it. The **44th Amendment (1978)** removed it from Part III. It is now a **legal (constitutional) right** under **Article 300A**: no person can be deprived of property except by authority of law.

The **National Human Rights Commission** was set up in **1993**. It inquires into violations of human rights and recommends action. It cannot punish; punishment is for the courts.

sections.heading: 5. Directive Principles of State Policy
sections.body_md:
The **Directive Principles** are in **Part IV** (Articles 36 to 51). They are guidelines for the government in making laws and policies. They are **non-justiciable**: courts cannot enforce them. They are, however, fundamental in the governance of the country.

- **Goals:** welfare of the people; social, economic and political justice; a higher standard of living; fair distribution of resources; international peace.
- **Policies:** a uniform civil code (listed as one principle); prohibition of intoxicants; cottage industries; care of useful cattle; village panchayats.
- **Non-justiciable rights:** adequate livelihood; equal pay for equal work for men and women; protection against economic exploitation; the right to work; early childhood care and education for children below six.

key_terms.definition_md: Guidelines in Part IV for the government in making laws and policies; they cannot be enforced by courts.

sections.heading: 6. Rights, principles and duties
sections.body_md:
**Rights restrain** the government; **principles direct** it. Rights protect **individuals**; principles promote the **welfare of society**. Conflicts arose, for example over **property and land reform**, and amendments followed. Courts have tried to read the two in **harmony**; the **Minerva Mills** case (1980) is cited in this connection.

**Fundamental Duties (Article 51A):** added by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**, with ten duties. The **86th Amendment (2002)** added an eleventh: a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to a child aged 6 to 14. Examples: respect the Constitution, the National Flag and the Anthem; protect and improve the natural environment; safeguard public property; develop scientific temper. Duties are not enforceable in the way rights are. (As of 2024, there are eleven duties.)

key_terms.definition_md: Obligations of citizens listed in Article 51A of the Constitution; they are not enforceable in the way rights are.
The approach of courts that reads the Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles together, so that neither is wholly ignored.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling property a Fundamental Right today: since 1978 it is a legal right under Article 300A.
- Mixing up the writs: habeas corpus (produce the person), mandamus (do the duty), prohibition (stop), quo warranto (by what authority), certiorari (quash).
- Saying Directive Principles are enforceable: they are non-justiciable.
- Writing that the Fundamental Duties were added in 1978: it was 1976.

**Tips:** give the Article number with each right; define each key term in one line; for a five-mark comparison give five separate points; use a short imagined example to show application.

questions.stem_md: A list of rights set out in a constitution, which the government is not allowed to violate, is described as a

options.text_md: charter of duties
bill of rights
directive list
preamble clause

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** bill of rights. A bill of rights lists the basic rights of citizens and places them beyond the reach of ordinary government action. In India these are the Fundamental Rights of Part III. A list of duties, a set of directives and the Preamble do not play this role.

questions.stem_md: Fundamental Rights are called justiciable. This means that

options.text_md: they can be taken away only by a judge
they apply only to persons who have been tried in court
they are a list of goals for the government to pursue
a citizen can go to a court to have them enforced

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a citizen can go to a court to have them enforced. Justiciable means enforceable by courts: a person whose right is violated can seek a remedy from a court. The other options misstate the term; goals for the government describe the Directive Principles, not Fundamental Rights.

questions.stem_md: In which Part of the Constitution are the Fundamental Rights placed?

options.text_md: Part III
Part I
Part IV
Part V

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Part III. Fundamental Rights are in Part III. Part IV holds the Directive Principles; Part I deals with the Union and its territory, and Part V with the Union government.

questions.stem_md: The owner of Sagar Tea House in the imagined town of Pallavpur refuses to serve a customer because of the customer's caste. Which Fundamental Right is the owner's act against?

options.text_md: Right to Freedom of Religion
Right against Exploitation
Right to Equality
Cultural and Educational Rights

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Right to Equality. The Right to Equality bars discrimination on grounds such as caste, and covers equal access to shops, restaurants and public places. No religion, forced labour or minority institution is involved, so the other rights are not the issue.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined village of Hariyal, a panchayat order bars families of one community from the common hand pump, calling them impure. The order is invalid mainly because the Constitution

options.text_md: gives every village the right to settle its own customs
makes water supply a Directive Principle only
abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form
allows restrictions on movement for reasons of custom

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form. Article 17 abolishes untouchability, and its practice in any form is an offence. A village has no right to override this, and the Directive Principles do not permit such an order. Reasonable restrictions on movement concern public order and similar grounds, never custom.

questions.stem_md: Students of the imagined Lakshya College gather peacefully and without weapons in a hall to discuss library hours. Which freedom are they using?

options.text_md: Freedom to assemble peacefully
Freedom to practise any profession
Freedom of residence in any part of the country
Freedom to move freely throughout the country

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Freedom to assemble peacefully. A peaceful meeting without arms is the exercise of the freedom of assembly under Article 19. Profession, residence and movement are other freedoms in the same Article but are not involved here.

questions.stem_md: A district authority in the imagined town of Kharbagh limits loudspeakers to before ten at night near a hospital. A shopkeeper objects that this violates the freedom of speech. Which reading is closest to the Constitution?

options.text_md: The freedom of speech is absolute and cannot be limited in any way
Speech made by a shopkeeper is outside the freedoms of Article 19
Only the Supreme Court can limit speech in any place
The freedom is real but not absolute; it can face reasonable restrictions such as public order

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The freedom is real but not absolute; it can face reasonable restrictions such as public order. Article 19 freedoms are subject to reasonable restrictions on grounds such as public order, decency and security of the State. A timing rule for noise near a hospital can be a reasonable restriction. The freedom is not absolute, it belongs to every citizen, and restrictions are made by law and not only by the Supreme Court.

questions.stem_md: Article 21A, which provides for free and compulsory education, covers children in the age group of

options.text_md: 3 to 18 years, added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976
6 to 14 years, added by the 86th Amendment in 2002
6 to 14 years, added by the 44th Amendment in 1978
5 to 16 years, present from the start in 1950

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 6 to 14 years, added by the 86th Amendment in 2002. Article 21A covers children aged 6 to 14 and was inserted by the 86th Amendment (2002). The 42nd Amendment added the Fundamental Duties and the 44th removed the right to property; neither added this Article, and the age band is not 3 to 18 or 5 to 16.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined town of Tirunagar, Kavita's brother is arrested at noon on Monday and kept at a police post until Wednesday evening without being taken before any magistrate. Which safeguard has been disregarded?

options.text_md: The safeguard of being produced before a magistrate within twenty-four hours of arrest
The right to be given a government job after release
The right to a free hearing within seven days
The right to choose which court will try the case

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The safeguard of being produced before a magistrate within twenty-four hours of arrest. Article 22 requires that an arrested person be produced before the nearest magistrate within twenty-four hours, excluding travel time, and be told the grounds of arrest. The other options are rights that do not exist in the Constitution.

questions.stem_md: Which statement describes preventive detention?

options.text_md: Detaining a person after conviction for a serious crime
Detaining a person on suspicion that he or she may act in a way harmful to security or public order
Detaining a person for questioning for no more than an hour
Detaining a person only after a magistrate finds him or her guilty

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Detaining a person on suspicion that he or she may act in a way harmful to security or public order. Preventive detention allows detention to stop a feared act in future, not to punish a past one, and it is hedged by safeguards in Article 22. Detention after conviction is punishment, and the other options describe ordinary custody or a guilty verdict, which are different.

questions.stem_md: A contractor in the imagined district of Naharpur makes labourers work long hours without pay to settle an old debt and does not let them leave. Which Fundamental Right is violated?

options.text_md: Right to Constitutional Remedies
Cultural and Educational Rights
Right against Exploitation
Right to Freedom of Religion

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Right against Exploitation. Forced and unpaid labour, called begar, and traffic in human beings are banned by Articles 23 and 24 under the Right against Exploitation. The Right to Constitutional Remedies is how a victim would seek relief, not the right that was violated.

questions.stem_md: A firecracker unit in the imagined town of Agnipur employs a twelve-year-old to pack explosive powder. Which provision does this go against?

options.text_md: The right of children to attend school only after age 14
The freedom of children to choose any profession
The right of minors to run an educational institution
The ban on employing children below 14 in factories and hazardous work

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The ban on employing children below 14 in factories and hazardous work. Article 24 prohibits employing children below 14 in factories, mines and other hazardous work. Choosing a profession is a freedom of citizens that does not make hazardous child work lawful, and the other two statements are not constitutional provisions.

questions.stem_md: A government-funded school in the imagined town of Devgarh requires all pupils, whatever their faith, to join a daily worship of one religion. Which right is affected?

options.text_md: Right to Equality before law
Right to Constitutional Remedies
Right against Exploitation
Right to Freedom of Religion

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Right to Freedom of Religion. Article 28 says no one can be compelled to take part in religious instruction or worship in an institution funded wholly by the State. This belongs to the Right to Freedom of Religion. Equality and exploitation are not the central issue, and Article 32 is only the remedy.

questions.stem_md: A linguistic community living in the imagined district of Sundari wants to set up its own school to keep its mother tongue and script alive. Which right supports this?

options.text_md: Right to Freedom, because of the freedom of profession
Right against Exploitation
Cultural and Educational Rights
Right to Equality in public employment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Cultural and Educational Rights. Articles 29 and 30 protect the language, script and culture of any section of citizens and let minorities, religious or linguistic, set up and run educational institutions. Freedom of profession and public employment concern different matters.

questions.stem_md: Which Article lets a person approach the Supreme Court directly when a Fundamental Right is violated?

options.text_md: Article 14
Article 32
Article 21
Article 44

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Article 32. Article 32 is the Right to Constitutional Remedies. Article 14 is equality before law, Article 21 protects life and personal liberty, and Article 44 is a Directive Principle.

questions.stem_md: Dr B. R. Ambedkar regarded Article 32 as the most important Article because

options.text_md: without a way to enforce them, the other rights would remain mere declarations
it lists all the rights that citizens may claim
it keeps the Supreme Court free from the government
it gives Parliament power to amend every right

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** without a way to enforce them, the other rights would remain mere declarations. A right is only as strong as the remedy behind it; Article 32 gives that remedy, so it makes the other rights real. It does not itself list the rights, it is not about judicial independence, and it does not give Parliament such a power.

questions.stem_md: Meena of the imagined town of Raighat says that her son has been held by police in an unknown place for three days with no charge. Which writ should she seek?

options.text_md: Mandamus
Habeas corpus
Quo warranto
Certiorari

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Habeas corpus. Habeas corpus, meaning to have the body, orders that a detained person be produced before the court so the legality of the detention can be examined. Mandamus orders an official to do a duty, quo warranto questions a public office, and certiorari quashes an order of a lower body.

questions.stem_md: The registrar of the imagined municipality of Vikrampur keeps refusing, without any reason, to issue a birth certificate that the law requires him to issue. The High Court orders him to perform this duty. This is a writ of

options.text_md: prohibition
habeas corpus
quo warranto
mandamus

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** mandamus. Mandamus, meaning we command, directs a public official to perform a legal duty. Prohibition stops a lower court from exceeding its authority, habeas corpus concerns a person in detention, and quo warranto questions the right to hold a public post.

questions.stem_md: A revenue tribunal in the imagined district of Mehrpur begins to try a criminal case that the law does not allow it to hear. Before it passes any order, the High Court directs it to stop. Which writ, and what does it do?

options.text_md: Prohibition, which stops a lower body from going beyond its jurisdiction
Certiorari, which cancels an order the lower body has already passed
Mandamus, which orders a lower body to act
Quo warranto, which removes a member from his office

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Prohibition, which stops a lower body from going beyond its jurisdiction. Prohibition is issued while proceedings are on, to stop a lower court or tribunal from acting beyond its authority. Certiorari comes after an order has been passed and quashes it. Mandamus compels action and quo warranto questions a person's right to an office, so neither fits.

questions.stem_md: A petitioner in the imagined state of Dharmapur argues that the person named vice-chancellor of a state university lacks the qualifications that the law requires for the post. Which writ asks by what authority the person holds the office?

options.text_md: Habeas corpus
Mandamus
Quo warranto
Prohibition

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Quo warranto. Quo warranto means by what authority; it tests whether a person holds a public office lawfully, and the court can remove one who does not qualify. Habeas corpus relates to detention, mandamus to a duty, and prohibition to a lower court exceeding its power.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the right to property is correct today?

options.text_md: It is a Fundamental Right under Article 19
It has been removed from the Constitution altogether
It is a legal right under Article 300A, no longer a Fundamental Right
It is a Directive Principle of State Policy

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It is a legal right under Article 300A, no longer a Fundamental Right. The 44th Amendment (1978) removed the right to property from the Fundamental Rights, and Article 300A now says that no person can be deprived of property except by authority of law. It still remains a constitutional right of a legal kind, so it was not scrapped, and it is not in Part IV.

questions.stem_md: Which statement fits the National Human Rights Commission, set up in 1993?

options.text_md: It inquires into violations of human rights and recommends action, but cannot itself punish
It tries and punishes officials who violate Fundamental Rights
It decides disputes between the Union and the States
It issues writs to enforce Fundamental Rights

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It inquires into violations of human rights and recommends action, but cannot itself punish. The Commission is a statutory body that investigates complaints, studies safeguards and recommends action. It does not punish, since punishing and issuing writs belong to courts, and it does not settle disputes between governments.

questions.stem_md: Directive Principles of State Policy are called non-justiciable. This means that

options.text_md: they have no force in law or in the work of government
they can be enforced only by the Supreme Court
they apply only to private citizens and not to the State
courts cannot enforce them, though they are fundamental in governance

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** courts cannot enforce them, though they are fundamental in governance. Non-justiciable means that a person cannot ask a court to enforce them. They are still described as fundamental in governing the country, and they are addressed to the State, so they are neither without force nor limited to the Supreme Court.

questions.stem_md: The imagined state of Marenpur passes a law to strengthen village councils and give them powers of self-government. Which kind of provision does this reflect?

options.text_md: A Fundamental Right, on freedom of association
A Directive Principle, on organising village panchayats
A Fundamental Duty, on safeguarding public property
A writ, on enforcing a duty of an official

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A Directive Principle, on organising village panchayats. Organising village panchayats is one of the Directive Principles of Part IV. Freedom of association is a different right of individuals, a duty binds citizens and is not a law of a state, and a writ is a court order.

questions.stem_md: A manifesto in the imagined state of Ranjan promises equal pay for men and women who do the same work. Among the commonly taught groups of Directive Principles, this belongs among the

options.text_md: non-justiciable rights
goals of the State
policies on personal law
Fundamental Duties

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** non-justiciable rights. Equal pay for equal work for men and women is usually placed among the non-justiciable rights, with the right to work and an adequate livelihood. Goals are broad aims such as justice and peace, policies cover matters such as personal law and village councils, and duties bind citizens.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best brings out how the Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles differ?

options.text_md: Fundamental Rights direct the government, while Directive Principles restrain it
Fundamental Rights restrain the government, while Directive Principles direct it
Both can be enforced in court in the same way
Only Directive Principles protect individuals against the State

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Fundamental Rights restrain the government, while Directive Principles direct it. Rights are limits on what government may do and are enforced by courts. Directive Principles point the government towards goals and cannot be enforced in court. The other options reverse this or blur it.

questions.stem_md: Why did early land reform laws, which aimed at fairer sharing of land, run into trouble in court?

options.text_md: Land reform was prohibited by the Directive Principles
The Directive Principles had no place in any law
Landowners claimed that the laws violated their right to property, a Fundamental Right at the time
The Constitution gave states no power over land

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Landowners claimed that the laws violated their right to property, a Fundamental Right at the time. Laws aimed at fairer distribution (a Directive Principle goal) clashed with the then Fundamental Right to property, and the conflict led to amendments. The Directive Principles in fact favour fair distribution, and they do guide law-making.

questions.stem_md: In discussions of the two parts of the Constitution, the Minerva Mills case (1980) is cited for the idea that

options.text_md: the Directive Principles override every Fundamental Right
the Fundamental Rights may be removed by simple majority
the Directive Principles can be enforced by any citizen in court
the Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles must be balanced and read in harmony

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles must be balanced and read in harmony. The case is cited for the view that the two parts are to be harmonised, with neither wholly overriding the other. The other options either give one part total priority or say rights can be removed with ease, which is not how the courts have read the Constitution.

questions.stem_md: Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution by which Amendment?

options.text_md: The 44th Amendment, 1978
The 86th Amendment, 2002
The 1st Amendment, 1951
The 42nd Amendment, 1976

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The 42nd Amendment, 1976. The 42nd Amendment (1976) introduced Article 51A with ten duties. The 44th removed the right to property from Part III, and the 86th added Article 21A and the eleventh duty.

questions.stem_md: Students of the imagined Chinar School remove plastic waste from the banks of their town stream and plant saplings there. Which Fundamental Duty are they acting on?

options.text_md: To defend the country when called upon
To respect the National Flag and the Anthem
To protect and improve the natural environment
To provide opportunities for education to a child

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** To protect and improve the natural environment. Cleaning a stream and planting saplings is protecting and improving the natural environment, a duty under Article 51A. The other duties concern defending the country, respecting national symbols and, for parents or guardians, education of children.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the Fundamental Duties is correct?

options.text_md: They are enforceable by writs like the Fundamental Rights
They are moral and civic obligations of citizens, not enforceable in the way rights are
They bind only the government and not the citizen
They are listed in Part III with the Fundamental Rights

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** They are moral and civic obligations of citizens, not enforceable in the way rights are. Article 51A states duties of citizens, and unlike rights it does not by itself create a court remedy. It sits in Part IVA, not in Part III, and it is addressed to citizens.

questions.stem_md: The eleventh Fundamental Duty, added in 2002, requires

options.text_md: a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to a child aged 6 to 14
every citizen to pay taxes on time
every citizen to vote in each election
the State to give free housing to all

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to a child aged 6 to 14. The 86th Amendment (2002) added this duty alongside Article 21A. Paying taxes and voting are not listed as duties in Article 51A, and giving housing is not a duty of citizens.

questions.stem_md: The government of the imagined state of Taralpur opens free play-and-learn centres for children below six. This is the carrying out of

options.text_md: Article 21A, a Fundamental Right of children below six
a Directive Principle on early childhood care and education
a Fundamental Duty of every citizen
a writ of mandamus against the State

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a Directive Principle on early childhood care and education. Early childhood care and education for children below six is a Directive Principle. Article 21A, in contrast, covers ages 6 to 14 and is a Fundamental Right. A duty binds citizens, and mandamus is a court order.

questions.stem_md: Shanta of the imagined village of Bhoomipur asks a court to order her state to set up cottage-industry centres, relying only on a Directive Principle. What is the likely position?

options.text_md: The court must order the centres to be set up at once
The petition fails because the principle has no value in governance
The petition must be heard first by Parliament
The court cannot enforce the principle directly, though the government is expected to follow it in policy

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The court cannot enforce the principle directly, though the government is expected to follow it in policy. Directive Principles are non-justiciable, so a court will not compel the State to act on one alone. They are still meant to guide laws and policy. The court is not required to order the centres, and Parliament does not decide such petitions.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a goal among the Directive Principles?

options.text_md: Fair distribution of resources among the people
Freedom to profess any religion
Protection against arrest without information of grounds
Right to move the Supreme Court

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Fair distribution of resources among the people. Fair distribution of resources, social and economic justice and international peace are goals of the Directive Principles. The remaining options are Fundamental Rights from Articles 25, 22 and 32.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A person whose Fundamental Right is violated can seek relief from a court.

**Reason (R):** Fundamental Rights are justiciable, and Article 32 gives the right to approach the Supreme Court.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both statements are true, and R explains A: because the rights are justiciable and Article 32 provides a remedy, a court can be approached.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The freedom of speech and expression is not absolute.

**Reason (R):** The Constitution allows reasonable restrictions on the Article 19 freedoms in the interest of matters such as public order.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: since restrictions on grounds like public order are allowed, the freedom has limits.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The right to property is no longer a Fundamental Right.

**Reason (R):** The 44th Amendment of 1978 removed it from Part III and made it a legal right under Article 300A.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: the 44th Amendment is the reason the right stands outside Part III today.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A court cannot order the government to carry out a Directive Principle on its own.

**Reason (R):** Directive Principles play no part in governing the country.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true because the principles are non-justiciable. R is false: they are described as fundamental in the governance of the country and guide policy and law-making.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Fundamental Duties can be enforced through writs in the same way as Fundamental Rights.

**Reason (R):** Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: duties are obligations of citizens that are not enforceable like rights. R is true, since the 42nd Amendment of 1976 added them.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Article 24 forbids employing children below 14 in factories, mines and hazardous work.

**Reason (R):** The Fundamental Rights are placed in Part III of the Constitution.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but the place of the rights in Part III does not explain why Article 24 bans child labour in hazardous work; the reason is the aim of preventing exploitation.

questions.stem_md: The right to move the courts for enforcement of Fundamental Rights is itself listed among the Fundamental Rights.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Article 32, the Right to Constitutional Remedies, is itself a Fundamental Right in Part III.

questions.stem_md: Article 18 allows the State to confer hereditary titles of nobility on citizens.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Article 18 abolishes titles, with limited exceptions for military and academic distinctions; hereditary titles are not conferred.

questions.stem_md: Directive Principles can be enforced by a court like Fundamental Rights.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Directive Principles are non-justiciable; courts do not enforce them directly.

questions.stem_md: A landowner in the imagined state of Kothapur says that her right to property is still protected as a Fundamental Right under Part III.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The right to property was removed from Part III in 1978; it is now a legal right under Article 300A, not a Fundamental Right.

questions.stem_md: The writ of ___ asks a person holding a public office by what authority he or she holds it.
questions.solution_md: Quo warranto means by what authority; a court issues it to test the legality of a claim to a public office.

questions.stem_md: The Fundamental Rights are in Part ___ and the Directive Principles in Part ___ of the Constitution.
questions.solution_md: Part III holds the Fundamental Rights, and Part IV (Articles 36 to 51) holds the Directive Principles.

questions.stem_md: The ___ Amendment, passed in 1976, added the Fundamental Duties through Article 51A.
questions.solution_md: The 42nd Amendment of 1976 added Article 51A, which began with ten duties.

questions.stem_md: Match each group of Articles with the Fundamental Right it forms.

options.text_md: Articles 14 to 18
Articles 19 to 22
Articles 23 and 24
Articles 25 to 28
Articles 29 and 30
Article 32

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(t), (b)–(r), (c)–(q), (d)–(u), (e)–(s), (f)–(p). These are the six categories of Fundamental Rights, in the order of their Articles.

questions.stem_md: Match each writ with what it does.

options.text_md: Habeas corpus
Mandamus
Prohibition
Quo warranto

match_right.text_md: Asks by what authority a person holds a public office
Orders that a detained person be produced before the court
Stops a lower court from acting beyond its power
Orders a public official to perform a legal duty

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Each writ has its own purpose; certiorari, the fifth writ, quashes an order of a lower body.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these developments in the order in which they took place.

options.text_md: Article 21A is inserted for children aged 6 to 14
The right to property is removed from the Fundamental Rights
The National Human Rights Commission is set up
Fundamental Duties are added to the Constitution

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (b) → (c) → (a). The duties came in 1976, the property change in 1978, the Commission in 1993 and Article 21A in 2002.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Arrange these steps in the order in which they would happen when a citizen's Fundamental Right is violated.

options.text_md: The authority is bound to obey the court's order
The court hears the case and issues a suitable writ
The person approaches the High Court or the Supreme Court
An official or authority violates the person's right

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (c) → (b) → (a). A violation comes first, followed by the petition, the hearing with a writ, and finally compliance.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: What are Fundamental Rights? Why are they called justiciable?
questions.solution_md: A definition (Part III, basic rights) and the meaning of justiciable.

answer.model_answer_md: **Fundamental Rights** are the basic rights of citizens listed in **Part III** of the Constitution, which the government cannot violate. They are **justiciable**, meaning a court can **enforce** them when they are violated.

marking_scheme.step: Definition: basic rights in Part III

questions.stem_md: Explain any two writs that the Supreme Court and the High Courts can issue.
questions.solution_md: Any two of the five writs, each with a standard meaning.

answer.model_answer_md: **Habeas corpus** orders that a person held in custody be produced before the court so the legality of the detention can be examined. **Mandamus** directs a public official or body to perform a legal duty that it has failed to perform.

questions.stem_md: What are the Directive Principles of State Policy? State why a court cannot enforce them.
questions.solution_md: Definition of the principles and the meaning of non-justiciable.

answer.model_answer_md: The **Directive Principles** in **Part IV** are guidelines for the government in making laws and policies, aimed at justice and welfare. They are **non-justiciable**: a court cannot enforce them, though they are **fundamental in the governance** of the country.

marking_scheme.step: Guidelines to the State in Part IV

questions.stem_md: State two things that the Right against Exploitation prohibits.
questions.solution_md: Any two of the prohibitions in Articles 23 and 24.

answer.model_answer_md: It prohibits **traffic in human beings** and **begar**, or forced labour, under Article 23. It also prohibits **employing children below 14** in factories, mines and hazardous work, under Article 24.

questions.stem_md: How has the status of the right to property changed since 1978?
questions.solution_md: The 1978 removal from Part III and the present status.

answer.model_answer_md: The **44th Amendment (1978)** removed the right to property from the **Fundamental Rights**. It is now a **legal right** under **Article 300A**: a person cannot be deprived of property except by authority of law.

marking_scheme.step: Removed from Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment (1978)
Now a legal right under Article 300A

questions.stem_md: Mention any two Fundamental Duties of a citizen.
questions.solution_md: Any two duties from Article 51A, each stated in a sentence.

answer.model_answer_md: A citizen has the duty to **respect the Constitution, the National Flag and the Anthem**. A citizen also has the duty to **protect and improve the natural environment** and to **safeguard public property**.

questions.stem_md: Give two differences between the Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles.
questions.solution_md: Two differences, such as enforceability and purpose.

answer.model_answer_md: Fundamental Rights are **justiciable** and enforced by courts, but Directive Principles are **non-justiciable**. Rights **restrain** the government and protect individuals, while the principles **direct** the government to promote the welfare of society.

questions.stem_md: What does Article 21A provide, and which Amendment inserted it?
questions.solution_md: The content of the Article and the Amendment with its year.

answer.model_answer_md: **Article 21A** gives children aged **6 to 14** a Fundamental Right to free and compulsory education. It was inserted by the **86th Amendment**, passed in **2002**.

marking_scheme.step: Free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14

questions.stem_md: State the role of the National Human Rights Commission, set up in 1993.
questions.solution_md: Inquiry and recommendation, with awareness work.

answer.model_answer_md: The **National Human Rights Commission** inquires into complaints of **violation of human rights** and **recommends** action to the authorities. It also spreads awareness and studies safeguards, but it cannot itself punish.

marking_scheme.step: Inquires into violations of human rights
Recommends action; no power to punish

questions.stem_md: Explain, with the example of a procession in the imagined town of Mehkar, why the freedoms of Article 19 are subject to reasonable restrictions.
questions.solution_md: An application to the example and the reason for restrictions.

answer.model_answer_md: A procession in **Mehkar** can be asked to follow a route and a time fixed by the authorities. The freedoms are **not absolute**; they can be limited by **reasonable restrictions** for **public order** and the security of the State, so that one person's freedom does not harm others.

marking_scheme.step: Freedoms are not absolute; reasonable restrictions apply
Relates to the example and a ground such as public order

questions.stem_md: The High Court of the imagined state of Gomtipur hears two petitions. In one it stops a tribunal midway; in the other it cancels an order already passed. Distinguish between the writs of prohibition and certiorari that these show.
questions.solution_md: Prohibition stops proceedings; certiorari quashes an order already made.

answer.model_answer_md: **Prohibition** is issued by a higher court to stop a lower court or tribunal from going beyond its jurisdiction while proceedings are on. **Certiorari** is issued after the lower body has passed an order, and it **quashes** that order.

marking_scheme.step: Certiorari quashes an order already passed

questions.stem_md: Explain any three provisions of the Right to Equality (Articles 14 to 18).
questions.solution_md: Three provisions from the Articles, each stated.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Equality before law:** all persons receive equal protection of the laws.
2. **No discrimination** by the State on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, and **equal opportunity** in public employment.
3. **Abolition of untouchability** (Article 17) and of **titles** (Article 18).

questions.stem_md: List and explain any three freedoms guaranteed by Article 19, with the limit on them.
questions.solution_md: Three named freedoms and the note on restrictions.

answer.model_answer_md: Article 19 guarantees freedom of **speech and expression**, to **assemble peacefully**, to form **associations**, to **move freely** and **reside** anywhere, and to follow a **profession**. Any of these may be limited by **reasonable restrictions** on grounds such as public order.

questions.stem_md: A man is arrested in the imagined town of Nandanpur. State three safeguards that the Constitution gives him.
questions.solution_md: Three of the safeguards of Article 22 for an ordinary arrest.

answer.model_answer_md: He must be **told the grounds** of his arrest. He has the right to **consult a lawyer** of his choice. He must be **produced before a magistrate within twenty-four hours** of arrest, excluding the time of travel, and cannot be held longer without the magistrate's order.

marking_scheme.step: Produced before a magistrate within 24 hours

questions.stem_md: Describe three features of the Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25 to 28).
questions.solution_md: Any three features from Articles 25 to 28.

answer.model_answer_md: Every person may **profess, practise and propagate** a religion, subject to public order, morality and health. Religious groups may **manage their own affairs**. **No one can be forced to pay a tax** for a religion, and **no compulsory religious instruction** is allowed in an institution wholly funded by the State.

marking_scheme.step: Freedom to profess, practise and propagate, with limits

questions.stem_md: Describe the three groups into which the Directive Principles are commonly classified, with one example of each.
questions.solution_md: Goals, policies and non-justiciable rights, each with an example.

answer.model_answer_md: **Goals:** broad aims such as social, economic and political justice and international peace. **Policies:** guides for laws, for example organising village panchayats and promoting cottage industries. **Non-justiciable rights:** claims such as equal pay for equal work for men and women, an adequate livelihood and the right to work.

questions.stem_md: Explain how the relation between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles led to conflicts and how the courts have approached it.
questions.solution_md: The source of conflict, the effect (amendments) and the later harmonising approach.

answer.model_answer_md: **Conflict arose** where measures for a fairer distribution of resources, a Directive Principle goal, clashed with the then right to **property**, so laws on **land reform** were challenged and amendments followed. Over time the courts, as in the **Minerva Mills** case (1980), have tried to **read the two in harmony**, giving neither complete priority.

marking_scheme.step: Conflict over property and land reform
Courts read the two in harmony

questions.stem_md: Write three points about the Fundamental Duties.
questions.solution_md: Origin, examples and the question of enforceability.

answer.model_answer_md: They were added by the **42nd Amendment (1976)** as **Article 51A**, with ten duties; an eleventh was added by the **86th Amendment (2002)**. Examples are respecting the Constitution and the National Flag, protecting the environment and developing a scientific temper. Unlike rights, they are **not enforceable** in the same way.

marking_scheme.step: Added by the 42nd Amendment, with the 86th adding an eleventh

questions.stem_md: Explain the Right to Freedom, covering Articles 19 to 22 in your own words.
questions.solution_md: Cover the freedoms, restrictions, Articles 20 and 21, 21A and 22.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Article 19** gives citizens freedom of speech and expression, assembly, association, movement, residence and profession.
2. These are subject to **reasonable restrictions** for public order and security.
3. **Protection in respect of conviction** (Article 20) shields a person from unfair punishment.
4. **Article 21** protects life and personal liberty, and **Article 21A** gives children aged 6 to 14 free and compulsory education.

questions.stem_md: Describe the five writs that can be issued for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights, and the courts that may issue them.
questions.solution_md: One mark for each writ, with the courts mentioned within the answer.

answer.model_answer_md: The **Supreme Court** (Article 32) and the **High Courts** (Article 226) may issue writs. 1. **Habeas corpus:** produce a detained person. 2. **Mandamus:** compel an official to do a legal duty. 3. **Prohibition:** stop a lower court acting beyond its power. 4. **Quo warranto:** ask by what authority a public office is held. 5. **Certiorari:** quash an order of a lower body made without authority.

marking_scheme.step: Habeas corpus, with the Supreme Court and High Courts

questions.stem_md: A class of Chinar School prepares a chart for Constitution Day. Help them by comparing the Fundamental Rights with the Directive Principles of State Policy on five points: part, enforceability, role, beneficiary and relation.
questions.solution_md: One mark for each point of comparison.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Part:** the rights are placed in **Part III** and the principles in **Part IV** of the Constitution.
2. **Enforceability:** rights are **justiciable**, so a court can enforce them; principles are **non-justiciable**.
3. **Role:** rights **restrain** the government by saying what it may not do; principles **direct** it by saying what it should work for.
4. **Beneficiary:** rights protect **individuals**; principles promote the **welfare of society**.
5. **Relation:** conflicts arose, as over property and land reform, and the courts have tried to read the two in **harmony**.

questions.stem_md: Explain the meaning and the commonly taught groups of the Directive Principles, with examples.
questions.solution_md: Meaning plus the three groups, with named examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Meaning:** guidelines in **Part IV** for laws and policy, **non-justiciable** but fundamental in governance.
2. **Goals:** justice, a higher standard of living, fair distribution of resources, international peace.
3. **Policies:** a **uniform civil code** as one listed principle, village panchayats, cottage industries.
4. **Other policies:** prohibition of intoxicants and care of useful cattle.
5. **Non-justiciable rights:** adequate livelihood, equal pay for equal work, right to work, early childhood care below six.

questions.stem_md: Some students argue that the Fundamental Duties are pointless because no court can punish a citizen for failing to perform them. Evaluate this view.
questions.solution_md: A balanced evaluation with both sides and a reasoned conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Origin:** the duties came through the **42nd Amendment (1976)**, with an eleventh added in **2002**.
2. **For the view:** they are **not enforceable** like rights, so there is no direct remedy.
3. **Against:** they remind citizens that **rights go with responsibilities**.
4. **Use:** courts and laws may refer to them while interpreting laws.
5. **Judgement:** their value is moral and civic, so they matter even without punishment.

questions.stem_md: Trace how the right to property moved from a Fundamental Right to a legal right and explain why it caused conflict.
questions.solution_md: The earlier status, the conflict, the 1978 change and the present status.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **At first** the right to property was a **Fundamental Right**.
2. **Land reform** aimed at fair distribution of land, a Directive Principle goal.
3. **Conflict:** landowners claimed that such laws violated their right, so **courts** struck some laws and **amendments** followed.
4. The **44th Amendment (1978)** removed it from Part III.
5. It is now a **legal right under Article 300A**: property can be taken only by authority of law.

questions.stem_md: Read the letter and answer the questions that follow. *(An imagined letter written by SOYL for practice; the writer and the town are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Article 22 sets out the safeguards on arrest and detention.

**(b)** Either missing safeguard, informing of the grounds or production before a magistrate within twenty-four hours, is acceptable.

**(c) (i)** Name the term and contrast it with punitive detention.

**OR (c) (ii)** The writ and the two courts.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Article 22**.

**(b)** The person was not **informed of the grounds** of the arrest (and was not produced before a magistrate).

**(c) (i)** It is **preventive detention**: detaining a person on suspicion of a possible future act harmful to public order. Detention after a trial is **punishment** for an offence already proved.

**OR (c) (ii)** They could seek **habeas corpus**, which asks that the person be produced and the **legality** of the detention examined. It can be issued by the **High Court** under Article 226 or the **Supreme Court** under Article 32.
